source_name: LTB Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations
text: Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 requires a landlord to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and to comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. This covers the everyday repair and pest problems tenants actually run into: mold or damp, cockroach, bedbug or other pest infestations, a broken furnace, heater or air conditioner, no heat in winter, leaking ceilings, plumbing leaks or broken pipes, broken or non-working smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detectors or fire alarm systems, broken appliances that came with the unit, structural damage, or unsafe conditions. Section 29(1) allows a tenant to apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) to determine whether a landlord has breached these obligations. A tenant must show that the premises are not in a good state of repair, are unfit for habitation, or that the landlord failed to comply with applicable health, safety, housing or maintenance standards; any one of these justifies a finding of breach, and it does not matter whether the landlord was ever asked to fix the problem before. Under section 30, the Board may order the landlord to do specified repairs or replacements within a specified time, allow the tenant to do the repairs and be reimbursed, reduce or suspend rent as compensation (an abatement), terminate the tenancy in serious cases (particularly where the unit is not fit for human habitation), order monetary compensation for damaged property or reasonable out-of-pocket expenses, restrict future rent increases until repairs are completed, or make any other order it considers appropriate, including interim orders.

topic: Landlord's right of entry / unauthorized or unannounced entry
source_name: LTB Interpretation Guideline 19: The Landlord's Right of Entry into a Rental Unit
text: This section covers a landlord walking into a tenant's unit unannounced, letting themselves in without knocking, entering while the tenant is home, asleep, or out, or letting in a contractor, repair person, cleaner, inspector, or another person without telling the tenant in advance. Under section 26 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a landlord may enter a rental unit without any advance notice only in an emergency, with the tenant's consent given at the time of entry, for regular cleaning if required by the tenancy agreement (between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.), or to show the unit to prospective tenants after a notice of termination has been given, provided the landlord makes reasonable efforts to inform the tenant in advance. A landlord may NOT enter without notice to perform repairs, even repairs the tenant requested, unless the tenant consents at the time. Under section 27, a landlord may enter with 24 hours' written notice specifying the reason, date, and a time between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m., for repairs or replacements, mortgage or insurance inspections, professional inspections, maintenance inspections, showing the unit to potential purchasers, or another reasonable reason set out in the tenancy agreement. Section 36.1(4) covers notice requirements for air conditioner inspections. A landlord entering repeatedly, entering without any notice outside these narrow exceptions, or coming in whenever they feel like it because they own the building is unauthorized entry, and a tenant does not have to let them in when these requirements haven't been met.

topic: Harassment, threats, illegal lockouts, and withholding vital services (heat, water, electricity)
text: Section 21 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 prohibits a landlord from withholding or cutting off a vital service such as heat, fuel, electricity, gas, or water -- for example shutting off the power or hot water because rent is late or because of a complaint. Section 22 prohibits substantial interference with a tenant's reasonable enjoyment of the unit. Section 23 prohibits harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats, or intimidation by the landlord, including yelling at a tenant, sending threatening messages, pressuring a tenant to move out early, or threatening to report a tenant to immigration authorities. Section 24 prohibits a landlord from changing the locks on a unit without immediately giving the tenant a replacement key -- an illegal lockout. Section 29(1) allows a tenant to apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for any of these rights violations. Harassment is defined, drawing on the Ontario Human Rights Code, as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. Under section 31, the Board may order rent abatement, administrative fines of up to $25,000, compensation for damaged or disposed property, reimbursement of reasonable out-of-pocket expenses, termination of the tenancy and eviction of the landlord in landlord-caused breach situations, or a cease-and-desist order against specified conduct, or any other order it considers appropriate. Section 41(2) requires that a tenant be given 72 hours of access to the property to remove belongings after a Sheriff's eviction. The general limitation period for most section 29 claims is one year from the date of the alleged breach.

topic: Rent deposit / last month's rent deposit rules
source_name: LTB Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act (About rent)
text: A landlord may collect a rent deposit from a new tenant on or before the start of a new tenancy. For a tenant who pays rent monthly, the deposit cannot be more than one month's rent; for a tenant who pays weekly, it cannot be more than one week's rent. The deposit can only be used as the rent payment for the last month or week before the tenant moves out -- it cannot be used for anything else, such as repairing damage, covering a stain on the carpet, or cleaning costs. The landlord must pay the tenant interest on the deposit every year, at a rate matching the annual rent increase guideline. If the landlord increases the rent, they may request that the tenant top up the deposit proportionally. A landlord who refuses to return an improperly-withheld deposit, refuses to apply it to the last month's rent, or tries to use it for something other than last month's rent, is in breach of the Act and a tenant can raise this with the Board.
